title: Nutritional significance of amino acids, vitamins and minerals as nutraceuticals in poultry production and health – a comprehensive review

subsections.section_title: Foundations and Scope of Nutraceuticals in Poultry Production
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging Delivery Platforms and Advanced Nutraceutical Formulations
subsections.content:
Emerging delivery platforms are reshaping how nutraceuticals are deployed in poultry systems by addressing three persistent constraints of conventional supplementation: instability during feed processing, poor gastrointestinal bioaccessibility, and imprecise delivery to the embryo or target tissue. Nano-enabled and bio-based carriers—including nanoemulsions, liposomes, micelles, solid lipid nanoparticles, polysaccharide matrices, and mesoporous materials—can improve solubility, protect labile compounds from oxidation or digestion, and enable controlled release of vitamins, amino acids, antioxidants, and trace minerals ref [1], ref [2]. In broader nutraceutical science, these systems have been developed specifically to enhance bioavailability, preserve bioactivity, and reduce the dose required for physiological efficacy, concepts that are directly relevant to poultry feeds, water-administered supplements, and hatchery interventions ref [1], ref [2].

In poultry, advanced formulation strategies are especially promising for compounds with narrow stability windows or low absorption efficiency, such as fat-soluble vitamins, methionine-related antioxidants, selenium, and phytogenic bioactives. Encapsulation can reduce antagonistic interactions within the feed matrix, minimize leaching or degradation during storage, and improve intestinal delivery under variable pH conditions ref [1], ref [2]. Beyond oral administration, in ovo delivery represents a high-value platform for precision nutraceutical programming of the embryo. Evidence that in ovo administration of sulfur-containing amino acids attenuated heat-stress biomarkers, improved antioxidant indices, and upregulated glutathione peroxidase-related responses in newly hatched broilers supports the broader rationale for embryo-targeted nutraceutical delivery ref [19].

Nevertheless, translation of these technologies into commercial poultry production requires careful attention to carrier composition, particle size, release kinetics, residue behavior, and regulatory safety. Reviews of nanomaterial use in dietary supplements emphasize that improved absorption must be balanced against toxicological uncertainty and the need for rigorous characterization of nanoformulations ref [1], ref [2]. Accordingly, the next generation of poultry nutraceuticals is likely to combine efficacy-oriented formulation design with safety-by-design principles, favoring biodegradable, food-grade, and application-specific platforms for heat stress management, gut health support, and micronutrient optimization ref [1], ref [2], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Foundations and Scope of Nutraceuticals in Poultry Production
subsections.subsection_title: Defining Nutraceuticals and Their Relevance to Poultry Production
subsections.content:
The term nutraceutical remains conceptually contested. Aronson argued that no internationally accepted definition adequately separates nutraceuticals from foods, fortified foods, dietary supplements, or medicinal products, and recommended more precise terminology instead of using a vague umbrella label ref [4]. For poultry science, however, the term still has practical value as a functional category for feed-derived bioactive compounds that deliver benefits beyond meeting basal nutrient requirements, especially when discussing amino acids, vitamins, minerals, probiotics, phytogenics, organic acids, and related feed additives ref [5].

In poultry production, nutraceutical relevance is tightly linked to the post-antibiotic-growth-promoter era. Reviews of antibiotic alternatives describe nutraceuticals as dietary tools that can stabilize gut ecology, improve mucosal barrier function, modulate immunity, and sustain growth performance under commercial stressors ref [5], ref [6]. This framing is particularly important because antibiotic restriction has intensified interest in non-antibiotic interventions that preserve health and productivity while limiting antimicrobial resistance pressures ref [6]. At the same time, evidence from raised-without-antibiotics systems indicates that removing antimicrobial tools without effective alternatives may increase welfare risks and disease burden, underscoring the need for robust nutraceutical strategies rather than simple ingredient substitution ref [7].

Accordingly, in this review nutraceuticals are treated operationally as nutritional bioactives or feed-associated compounds used at physiological or supranutritional levels to support performance, resilience, and health in poultry. Their relevance extends from gut health and pathogen control to oxidative balance, stress mitigation, skeletal integrity, and immune competence, thereby positioning essential amino acids, vitamins, and minerals not only as nutrients but also as functional modulators of poultry biology ref [5], ref [6]. This functional definition is especially useful for evaluating evidence across conventional, antibiotic-reduced, and antibiotic-free production systems ref [7], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Foundations and Scope of Nutraceuticals in Poultry Production
subsections.subsection_title: Gut Health, Microbiota Modulation, and Antibiotic Alternatives
subsections.content:
Gut health is central to poultry productivity because the intestinal epithelium, mucus layer, immune system, and microbiota jointly regulate nutrient digestion, barrier function, and pathogen resistance. Early microbial succession after hatch strongly shapes this ecosystem, while dysbiosis diverts nutrients toward inflammation, increases toxic fermentation products, and depresses feed efficiency and growth ref [9]. Consequently, nutraceutical strategies that stabilize microbial ecology are now integral to antibiotic-reduction programs in poultry ref [9], ref [10].

Among these strategies, probiotics remain the most established. They act through competitive exclusion, antagonism against enteropathogens, modulation of digestive activity, and stimulation of mucosal and systemic immunity ref [8], ref [10]. In poultry, probiotic supplementation has been associated with reduced Salmonella and Campylobacter colonization, improved cecal microflora composition, enhanced villus architecture, and better performance, although responses are strain-, dose-, and management-dependent ref [8], ref [9]. Prebiotics and synbiotics complement these effects by selectively enriching beneficial taxa, increasing short-chain fatty acid production, and reinforcing immune tolerance and epithelial integrity ref [9], ref [10].

As in-feed antibiotic growth promoters have been restricted, phytogenic compounds and microbiota-directed additives have gained relevance as antibiotic alternatives. Cinnamon oil, rich in cinnamaldehyde and related phenolics, shows antimicrobial activity against E. coli, Salmonella, and other poultry pathogens while often increasing Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium abundance and improving feed conversion and antioxidant status ref [11]. Importantly, gut-modulating additives may also alter drug disposition; dietary probiotic or prebiotic inclusion increased florfenicol exposure and tissue persistence in broilers, underscoring the need to integrate microbiome-targeted nutraceuticals with antimicrobial stewardship and residue management ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Foundations and Scope of Nutraceuticals in Poultry Production
subsections.subsection_title: Antioxidants, Trace Minerals, and Stress Physiology
subsections.content:
Oxidative stress is a central physiological consequence of heat load in poultry, linking mitochondrial ROS overproduction with lipid peroxidation, endocrine perturbation, immune dysfunction, and reduced growth and carcass yield. Antioxidant nutraceuticals therefore act not only as radical scavengers, but as modulators of stress physiology. A recent review shows that supranutritional vitamin A, E, and C, together with Zn and Se, consistently improve redox balance and performance under high environmental temperature, with combined supplementation often outperforming single nutrients ref [13].

Trace minerals are especially relevant because they support endogenous antioxidant enzymes and stress-responsive pathways. Zinc and selenium contribute to Cu/Zn-superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase systems, respectively, while organic mineral sources generally show superior bioavailability and biological efficacy compared with inorganic salts. In broilers, organic trace mineral programs have been associated with better growth, carcass traits, and immune responses than inorganic forms ref [15]. Under heat stress, zinc-methionine improved weight gain, feed efficiency, protein utilization, glutathione peroxidase activity, humoral immunity, muscle Zn deposition, and reduced malondialdehyde, indicating tighter control of oxidative injury ref [17].

Beyond classical antioxidant indices, trace minerals can attenuate cellular stress signaling and barrier dysfunction. Water-delivered amino acid-chelated trace minerals reduced circulating corticosterone, HSP70, FITC-dextran leakage, and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in heat-stressed broilers, suggesting benefits at the gut–immune–stress axis ref [16]. Developmental programming may also contribute: in ovo methionine-cysteine administration during thermal challenge increased total antioxidant capacity and glutathione, lowered HSP90, and enhanced IGF-I, TLR4, and jejunal morphometry in hatchlings ref [8]. Collectively, antioxidants and bioavailable trace minerals function as practical nutraceutical tools to improve resilience, welfare, and productivity during environmental and metabolic stress ref [13], ref [15]-ref [17], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Foundations and Scope of Nutraceuticals in Poultry Production
subsections.subsection_title: Amino Acids as Functional Nutraceuticals in Poultry
subsections.content:
Amino acids in poultry nutrition should be viewed not only as substrates for protein accretion, but also as functional nutraceuticals that regulate intestinal repair, immune competence, and resilience to enteric stress. Trophic amino acids such as threonine, arginine, and glutamine are particularly relevant because the intestine has high nutrient demands and rapid epithelial turnover, especially during coccidiosis or necrotic enteritis challenge ref [18], ref [12]. More broadly, amino acids influence leukocyte activation, cytokine production, redox balance, and barrier maintenance, supporting the concept that requirement estimates based solely on growth may underestimate needs under commercial stress conditions ref [12].

Threonine is central to mucin synthesis and mucosal defense; higher dietary threonine improves gut morphology, supports Ig-related responses, and can enhance growth and immune performance when protein supply or sanitary conditions are suboptimal ref [10], ref [13], ref [18]. Arginine is indispensable in birds because of limited endogenous synthesis, and serves as a precursor for nitric oxide and polyamines, thereby linking vasoregulation, immune activation, and epithelial restitution ref [20], ref [12]. In challenged broilers, supplemental arginine attenuates villus damage and reduces inflammatory signaling during coccidial insult, indicating a clear nutraceutical role beyond growth promotion ref [25], ref [18].

Glutamine functions as a major fuel for enterocytes and immune cells and becomes conditionally essential during inflammation. Its supplementation has been associated with improved villus architecture, immune indices, and performance in broilers, particularly when intestinal integrity is compromised ref [22], ref [18], ref [12]. Sulfur amino acids also display functional benefits: methionine supports antioxidant defenses and immune responsiveness, while methionine or methionine dipeptide supplementation mitigates Eimeria-induced oxidative stress in the jejunum ref [24], ref [13]. Collectively, these data position selected amino acids as practical nutraceutical tools for precision support of gut health, immunity, and recovery in antibiotic-constrained poultry systems ref [18], ref [20], ref [22].

Vitamin–mineral interactions in poultry are best understood within an integrated antioxidant network rather than as isolated nutrient effects. Selenium is central to this network because it supports selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidases and thioredoxin reductases, while also sparing or recycling non-enzymatic antioxidants including vitamin E and glutathione; thus, Se status can modify responses to vitamin supplementation and oxidative challenge ref [26]. Under heat stress, combined use of antioxidant vitamins (A, E, C) with Zn and Se is generally more effective than single-nutrient supplementation for limiting lipid peroxidation, sustaining enzyme activity, and preserving performance ref [13].

Mechanistically, Zn, Cu and Mn act as structural or catalytic cofactors for antioxidant enzymes, whereas vitamins E and C function mainly as chain-breaking and recycling antioxidants. This complementarity explains why organic trace minerals often strengthen antioxidant defence despite lower inclusion rates than inorganic salts ref [16]. In layers, methionine hydroxy analog-chelated Cu/Mn/Zn increased carbonic anhydrase, ceruloplasmin and Mn-superoxide dismutase activities, while improving shell quality and mineral retention, indicating that mineral form influences both oxidative metabolism and productive traits ref [15].

Zinc–vitamin interactions are especially relevant during immune and thermal stress. Replacing inorganic Zn with zinc-methionine improved lymphocyte proportions, reduced heterophil:lymphocyte ratio, and enhanced vaccine and secondary antibody responses in broilers ref [17]. Under high ambient temperature, zinc-methionine further improved growth, protein utilization, glutathione peroxidase activity, meat Zn deposition, and reduced malondialdehyde, illustrating how organic Zn can amplify antioxidant and immune outcomes when birds face redox imbalance ref [19]. Collectively, these data support form-specific, combination-based vitamin–mineral strategies as a practical nutraceutical approach in poultry production ref [26], ref [13], ref [16].

subsections.subsection_title: Foundational and General Perspectives on Vitamin Use in Poultry Nutrition
subsections.content:
Vitamins are foundational nutraceuticals in poultry because they participate directly in energy metabolism, epithelial integrity, skeletal development, reproduction, antioxidant protection, and immune regulation; however, their practical value depends on bioavailability, ingredient stability, bird age, health status, and production objectives rather than simple inclusion above requirement tables ref [30], ref [32]. In cereal–soy diets, natural vitamin supply is variable and losses during ingredient storage, pelleting, oxidation, and prolonged feed handling can be substantial, which justifies routine premix use as a preventive nutritional strategy ref [30].

A general principle across poultry vitamin nutrition is that both deficiency and excess can impair performance and health. This is especially clear for vitamin A, where inadequate intake compromises mucosal barriers, antibody production, T-cell responsiveness, and resistance to bacterial, viral, and protozoal challenge, whereas excessive intake may also depress immunity and induce toxicity-related tissue damage ref [32]. Thus, vitamin supplementation should be viewed as optimization of physiological resilience, not merely correction of overt deficiency.

Foundational evidence also shows that vitamin responses are context dependent. Vitamin D is classically linked to calcium–phosphorus homeostasis and bone integrity, but its broader endocrine and immunomodulatory roles suggest that adequacy may influence disease resistance and metabolic robustness beyond rickets prevention ref [31]. More broadly, modern genotypes, intensive growth, environmental stress, and vaccination pressure may shift practical vitamin needs upward relative to minimal historical requirements, supporting the nutraceutical concept of targeted safety margins and strategic multivitamin fortification in commercial poultry systems ref [30], ref [31], ref [32].

Water-soluble vitamins in poultry nutraceutical programs are used less as classical deficiency preventives and more as metabolic and stress-modulating adjuncts. Vitamin C is the best studied example: although poultry can synthesize ascorbate, supplemental inclusion is repeatedly reported to improve growth, nutrient utilization, carcass quality, bone characteristics, and several immune indices under commercial or stressful conditions, particularly heat load [3], ref [38]. In broilers, graded dietary ascorbic acid increased weight gain and digestibility and improved selected lymphocyte subsets and post-vaccinal infectious bursal disease antibody titers, with benefits most evident at higher supplementation levels [3]. Under high stocking density, dietary vitamin C also improved performance, moderated adverse blood biochemical changes, and upregulated heat-shock-response transcripts, indicating a role in stress resilience [8].

Beyond ascorbate, evidence for other water-soluble vitamins supports targeted rather than indiscriminate use. Multivitamin administration in drinking water, especially when combined with enzymes, improved body weight and erythrocyte-related hematological indices in broilers, suggesting better nutrient utilization and metabolic status under field conditions [1]. In ovo delivery of vitamin C, pyridoxine, or cyanocobalamin in Japanese quail enhanced early growth, improved protein and lipid profiles, and increased thymus and bursa development, despite variable hatchability responses [10]. Thiamine has also been linked with altered energy metabolism, lower plasma triglycerides, and greater hepatic oxygen consumption, consistent with effects on oxidative metabolism and muscle accretion [12].

Vitamin B12 deserves particular attention in young waterfowl because of its hematopoietic role. In White Pekin ducks, supplemental cyanocobalamin did not markedly change weight gain over 21 d, but significantly improved leukocyte, erythrocyte, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet indices, supporting its value for blood formation and early physiological robustness [13]. Collectively, current evidence suggests that water-soluble vitamin supplementation is most defensible as a precision nutraceutical strategy during early life, incubation, heat or density stress, and periods of immune challenge, whereas routine blanket overuse remains insufficiently justified [3], ref [38], [10], [13].

subsections.subsection_title: Fat-Soluble Vitamins: A, D, E and K in Poultry Health and Productivity
subsections.content:
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K exert complementary effects on productivity, skeletal integrity, reproduction and immune competence in poultry, making them central nutraceutical tools in modern feeding programs. Vitamin A is essential for epithelial integrity, reproduction and immune regulation, yet its response is dose-dependent: moderate supplementation improved egg production and some immune indices in heat-stressed layers, whereas excessive inclusion in broiler breeders impaired eggshell quality, hatchability, liver-related indices and lymphocyte responses ref [18], ref [20]. These findings reinforce that vitamin A is beneficial within a physiologically appropriate range, but oversupply can become counterproductive ref [18], ref [20].

Vitamin D has the strongest evidence base for bone and mineral metabolism. In layers, supplemental vitamin D3, D2 or 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 improved calcium and phosphorus utilization, although effects on egg quality and bone mineral density were limited when basal Ca, P and vitamin D supply was already adequate ref [11]. In broilers, source and level are important: 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 generally supported superior growth, tibia ash and lower tibial dyschondroplasia than cholecalciferol at equivalent nominal activity, while vitamin D3 metabolites can also improve bone traits and, in some cases, meat quality ref [13], ref [14]. Beyond mineral homeostasis, vitamin D shows clear immunomodulatory activity in chickens, with effects shaped by dose and dietary calcium-phosphorus status ref [12].

Vitamin E functions primarily as a membrane-phase antioxidant, protecting lipids from peroxidation and supporting immune resilience under commercial stressors. Current perspectives emphasize that tocopherols and tocotrienols are not biologically redundant, and source or isoform may influence antioxidant potency and downstream physiological outcomes ref [47]. Vitamin K, although less discussed than A, D or E, is indispensable for osteocalcin carboxylation and bone mineralization; graded menadione supplementation improved bone breaking strength, mineral density and bone ash in broilers, with early growth appearing especially responsive ref [16]. Collectively, these vitamins should be viewed not as isolated additives but as interacting nutraceutical regulators of oxidative balance, mineral deposition, fertility and flock robustness.

subsections.section_title: Delivery Systems, Applications, and Translational Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Advanced Delivery Systems for Functional Nutrients
subsections.content:
Advanced delivery systems are increasingly used to overcome the instability, low aqueous solubility, poor intestinal dispersion, and variable bioavailability of many functional nutrients relevant to poultry, including vitamins, trace minerals, amino acids, and phytogenic compounds. Nanoformulations, nanoemulsions, liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and encapsulated mineral systems can protect labile actives during feed processing and gastrointestinal transit, enable controlled release, and improve epithelial uptake while potentially lowering required inclusion rates ref [1]. These principles are especially relevant for poultry, where rapid digesta passage and heterogeneous gut pH can limit the efficiency of conventional nutraceutical supplementation ref [48].

In poultry, nanoparticle-based supplementation has been associated with improved growth, antioxidant status, immune modulation, and pathogen control, although responses remain strongly material- and dose-dependent ref [48]. Reviews of commercial applications indicate promising outcomes for ZnO, Se, Cu, Ag, chitosan-based carriers, and calcium-phosphate nanoparticles, including better mineral utilization, enhanced immune indices, and reduced enteropathogen burden, but they also emphasize the need to balance efficacy with toxicological safety, tissue retention, and regulatory compliance ref [48]. Similar translational considerations have been highlighted more broadly for nanoformulated dietary supplements and foods, where particle size, surface properties, and carrier composition determine both bioaccessibility and risk profiles ref [1].

A practical example of advanced delivery in broilers is the feed supplementation of a formulation combining ascorbic acid with a solid dispersion of curcumin in polyvinylpyrrolidone plus boric acid, which significantly reduced Salmonella Enteritidis colonization and partially mitigated necrotic enteritis-associated intestinal dysfunction ref [49]. This study illustrates how dispersion engineering can enhance the biological action of poorly soluble phytochemicals and support synergistic combinations of antioxidant and antimicrobial nutraceuticals ref [49]. Overall, next-generation delivery platforms offer a credible route to precision nutraceutical use in poultry, but further work is needed on dose optimization, stability in commercial feed manufacture, residue-free safety, and cost-effective scale-up ref [1], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Delivery Systems, Applications, and Translational Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Targeted Nutrient Supplementation in Poultry Production
subsections.content:
Targeted nutrient supplementation in poultry production increasingly relies on precision matching of limiting amino acids and bioavailable trace minerals to genotype, diet composition, and physiological stress. In low-crude-protein programs, strategic inclusion of essential and nonessential amino acids can sustain growth while improving nitrogen efficiency, whereas inadequate methionine depresses gain and feed efficiency and alters amino-acid transporter expression and digestibility patterns, underscoring the need for functional rather than merely total amino acid formulation ref [54], ref [10]. Threonine is particularly responsive to diet context: requirements rise when protein digestibility is compromised, and supplementation above conventional recommendations improves feed conversion, villus architecture, ileal amino-acid digestibility, and immune organ development, especially in birds fed canola meal or other less digestible protein sources ref [51], ref [55].

A second axis of targeting concerns mineral source, dose, and antagonistic interactions. In phytase-supplemented diets, increasing zinc from marginal to moderate levels can improve body weight gain, phosphorus utilization, and net energy retention without suppressing phytase efficacy, although Zn retention patterns remain dose-dependent ref [23]. Likewise, organic and chelated trace minerals often outperform inorganic salts in growth, carcass traits, immune indices, and profitability, reflecting improved stability and reduced antagonism in the gut ref [14]. This is especially relevant under elevated copper, where chelated zinc supports superior feed intake and weight gain relative to inorganic Zn, indicating better resilience to mineral-mineral competition ref [9].

Targeted supplementation can also be used to steer carcass quality and immune competence. Methionine-lysine optimization, sometimes combined with L-carnitine, has been associated with improved growth efficiency and selective effects on carcass traits and vaccine-related immune responses, although responses depend on dose and background diet ref [11]. Collectively, these studies support a shift from fixed safety margins toward phase-specific, ingredient-sensitive, and source-specific nutrient delivery that integrates digestibility, bioavailability, and immunometabolic outcomes ref [14], ref [51], ref [23], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Delivery Systems, Applications, and Translational Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Functional Animal-Derived Foods and Biofortification Applications
subsections.content:
Functional animal-derived foods in poultry are most clearly exemplified by designer eggs and, increasingly, nutritionally modified meat products, in which feed formulation is used to enrich edible tissues with health-promoting compounds rather than merely to maximize production efficiency. This concept links poultry nutrition to public health by creating foods with altered lipid profiles, reduced cholesterol burden, or enhanced concentrations of vitamins, trace minerals, and antioxidant pigments [1], [3].

Among biofortification strategies, omega-3 enrichment is the most established. Inclusion of flaxseed, fish oil, microalgae, or stearidonic acid-rich oils can substantially increase yolk ALA, EPA, and DHA, although transfer efficiency depends strongly on source and dose and often plateaus at higher inclusion levels [3]. Parallel approaches have produced selenium-, vitamin E-, carotenoid-, lutein-, and zeaxanthin-enriched eggs, improving their value as carriers of nutrients that are frequently inadequate in human diets [1], [3]. Organic selenium is particularly effective for egg selenium fortification, while plant- and algae-derived pigments can enhance both yolk coloration and xanthophyll delivery [3].

Biofortification of poultry products also has translational relevance beyond nutrient adequacy. Designer eggs with improved n-6:n-3 ratios, added antioxidants, or lower yolk cholesterol have been positioned as functional foods for cardiovascular and ocular health, whereas emerging applications include enrichment with bioactives such as conjugated linoleic acid, phytoestrogen-related compounds, L-carnitine, GABA, and even egg-yolk antibodies (IgY) for immunonutritional use [3]. Nevertheless, commercial translation requires balancing enrichment efficacy, sensory quality, oxidative stability, production cost, and transparent labeling, especially because nutrient deposition into eggs or meat is biologically constrained and consumer acceptance depends on clearly demonstrated health benefit [1], [3].

subsections.section_title: Delivery Systems, Applications, and Translational Perspectives
subsections.subsection_title: Health Applications and Translational Potential of Functional Foods
subsections.content:
Functional foods have translational relevance for poultry not only as production tools, but also as health-modulating interventions that link nutrient delivery, gut integrity, immune competence, and downstream food quality. Broader functional-food literature emphasizes that bioactive nutrients act through interconnected antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic pathways rather than through simple nutrient replacement alone, a concept highly applicable to poultry exposed to heat stress, enteric challenge, and intensive production pressures ref [59], ref [5], ref [6]. In this context, amino acids, vitamins, trace minerals, probiotics, prebiotics, phytochemicals, and mixed nutraceutical formulations can be viewed as health-supportive components within a systems framework rather than isolated additives ref [5], ref [6].

A major translational opportunity lies in intestinal health. Reviews of nutraceuticals and gut-directed functional foods show that probiotic, prebiotic, and synbiotic strategies can stabilize microbiota, reinforce epithelial barrier function, and regulate mucosal immunity ref [5], ref [44], ref [52]. This aligns closely with poultry evidence that gut-focused nutraceuticals improve resilience against dysbiosis and inflammatory enteropathies, while amino acids such as threonine, glutamine, and arginine further support mucin synthesis, epithelial repair, and immune signaling ref [47], ref [48], ref [53], ref [36], ref [50]. Such integration is especially relevant to antibiotic-reduced systems, where nutritional modulation is increasingly expected to complement biosecurity and vaccination ref [32], ref [46].

From a One Health and consumer-health perspective, translational value also depends on evidence quality, safety, and realistic claims. Human functional-food scholarship consistently warns that these products are not panaceas and that benefit claims should rest on robust, reproducible data and attention to dose, matrix, and safety ref [6], ref [10]. For poultry, this argues for moving beyond performance-only endpoints toward validated biomarkers of oxidative stress, inflammation, intestinal function, and product nutritional quality, thereby enabling more credible translation from feed intervention to animal health benefit and, ultimately, to functional animal-derived foods with human relevance ref [59], ref [5], ref [42], ref [43].
